providers.description: Airtable records: read, create, update and delete a record in a base's table

credentials.name: airtable.access_token
credentials.description: Airtable access token sent as a bearer — a personal access token or an OAuth-issued one

operations.description: Read one record from a table — its cell values are under `fields` in the response, keyed by column name. Returns every column the token can see, in Airtable's default JSON cell format: narrowing or reformatting them needs the `fields[]` and `cellFormat` query parameters this connector cannot encode

parameters.name: base_id
parameters.description: The base's id, the `app…` segment in the base's URL in Airtable

parameters.name: table_id
parameters.description: The table's id, the `tbl…` segment in the table's URL in Airtable. Airtable also routes this segment on a table *name*, which this connector does not accept: a name is interpolated into the URL unencoded, so one containing a space or a `/` would address the wrong route

parameters.name: record_id
parameters.description: The record's id, `rec…`. It is what a create returns and what the record's own URL ends with

fields.description: The record's cell values, keyed by column name. Individual columns are not enumerated: they are the base's own schema, which differs per base and changes at runtime — recording the envelope is what a consumer cannot infer

id.description: The record's id

operations.flux:
op airtable-record-get(base_id: String, table_id: String, record_id: String) -> Any
  description "Read one record from a table — its cell values are under `fields` in the response, keyed by column name. Returns every column the token can see, in Airtable's default JSON cell format: narrowing or reformatting them needs the `fields[]` and `cellFormat` query parameters this connector cannot encode. A non-2xx response is returned as data, not a failure: the vendor's error message is at `/error/message`, its error code at `/error/type` in the response body."
  risk "low"
  idempotency "idempotent"
  effects ["network"]
  expose true

  base = "https://api.airtable.com"
  url = fmt("{base}/v0/{base_id}/{table_id}/{record_id}")
  response = http.request(method: "GET", url)
  return response

operations.description: Create one record in a table. Cell values are supplied under `fields`, keyed by column name, and must already be in the exact JSON form each column expects — Airtable's `typecast` coercion cannot be requested yet (see the connector's notes). The created record, with its `rec…` id, is in the response

parameters.name: base_id
parameters.description: The base's id, the `app…` segment in the base's URL in Airtable

parameters.name: table_id
parameters.description: The table's id, the `tbl…` segment in the table's URL in Airtable. The name form is not accepted — see `airtable-record-get`

parameters.name: cell_values
parameters.description: The record's cell values, as an object keyed by the table's column names — `{"Name": "Acme", "Status": "Open"}`. Each value must match its column's type: a single-select takes one of its configured option names, a linked-record column takes an array of `rec…` ids, a date takes an ISO 8601 string. An unknown column name is rejected, not ignored

schema.description: A map from column name to cell value. Untyped here because the columns are the base's own schema

cell_values.description: A map from column name to cell value. Untyped here because the columns are the base's own schema

fields.description: The created record's cell values as Airtable stored them, keyed by column name. Computed and formula columns appear here having been evaluated

id.description: The created record's id — what later calls address it by

operations.flux:
op airtable-record-create(base_id: String, table_id: String, cell_values: Any) -> Any
  description "Create one record in a table. Cell values are supplied under `fields`, keyed by column name, and must already be in the exact JSON form each column expects — Airtable's `typecast` coercion cannot be requested yet (see the connector's notes). The created record, with its `rec…` id, is in the response. A non-2xx response is returned as data, not a failure: the vendor's error message is at `/error/message`, its error code at `/error/type` in the response body."
  risk "medium"
  idempotency "non_idempotent"
  effects ["network"]
  expose true

  base = "https://api.airtable.com"
  url = fmt("{base}/v0/{base_id}/{table_id}")
  content_type = "application/json"
  payload = { fields: cell_values }
  response = http.request(body: payload, headers: { "content-type": content_type }, method: "POST", url)
  return response

operations.description: Update one record's cell values. The write is sparse: only the columns named in `fields` change and every other column of the record is left exactly as it was. Values must already be in the form each column expects — `typecast` coercion cannot be requested yet. The updated record is in the response

parameters.name: base_id
parameters.description: The base's id, the `app…` segment in the base's URL in Airtable

parameters.name: table_id
parameters.description: The table's id, the `tbl…` segment in the table's URL in Airtable. The name form is not accepted — see `airtable-record-get`

parameters.name: record_id
parameters.description: The id of the record to update

parameters.name: cell_values
parameters.description: The columns to change, as an object keyed by the table's column names. Columns not named here keep their current values. Setting a column to `null` clears it, which is the only way to empty a cell through this operation

schema.description: A map from column name to cell value. Untyped here because the columns are the base's own schema

cell_values.description: A map from column name to cell value. Untyped here because the columns are the base's own schema

createdTime.description: When the record was created — unchanged by an update

fields.description: The record's cell values after the update, keyed by column name. Every column is returned, not only the changed ones

id.description: The record's id

  effects ["network"]
  expose true

operations.description: Delete one record and every cell value in it. There is no API route back: Airtable's trash and revision history are UI features on a retention window, not endpoints, so a flux run cannot undo this. Responds `{"id": …, "deleted": true}`

parameters.name: base_id
parameters.description: The base's id, the `app…` segment in the base's URL in Airtable

parameters.name: table_id
parameters.description: The table's id, the `tbl…` segment in the table's URL in Airtable. The name form is not accepted — see `airtable-record-get`

parameters.name: record_id
parameters.description: The id of the record to delete

deleted.description: Always `true` on a 2xx. Airtable reports a record that was already gone as a 404 rather than as `false`

id.description: The id of the record that was deleted

operations.flux:
op airtable-record-delete(base_id: String, table_id: String, record_id: String) -> Any
  description "Delete one record and every cell value in it. A non-2xx response is returned as data, not a failure: the vendor's error message is at `/error/message`, its error code at `/error/type` in the response body."

  effects ["network"]

  base = "https://api.airtable.com"
  url = fmt("{base}/v0/{base_id}/{table_id}/{record_id}")
  response = http.request(method: "DELETE", url)
  return response

op babelforce-agent-list(page: Number, max: Number, q: String, enabled: Bool, name: String, number: String, sourceId: String, source: String, state: String, groupIds: Any, groups: Any) -> Any
  description "List and filter agents. Doubles as the verification operation — cheap, read-only, and it fails loudly on a bad credential; this API has no /me endpoint"

  effects ["network"]

  when max
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}max={max}")
    sep = "&"
  when q
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}q={q}")
    sep = "&"
  when enabled
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}enabled={enabled}")
    sep = "&"
  when name
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}name={name}")
    sep = "&"
  when number
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}number={number}")

  when sourceId
    url = fmt("{url}{sep}sourceId={sourceId}")

  when state

operations.description: Safe-update selected ticket fields against the caller's updated_stamp; at least one of status, priority, assignee_id, group_id or type must be supplied

parameters.name: ticket_id
parameters.description: The ticket id

parameters.name: updated_stamp
parameters.description: Optimistic-concurrency stamp: Zendesk rejects the update if the ticket moved since this stamp

parameters.name: safe_update
parameters.description: Constant `true` — not caller-supplied; it is what makes updated_stamp binding. Dropping it turns every write into a last-write-wins race

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: The ticket's status

parameters.name: priority
parameters.description: The ticket's priority

parameters.name: assignee_id
parameters.description: The agent the ticket is assigned to

parameters.name: group_id
parameters.description: The group the ticket belongs to

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: The ticket's type

audit.description: What this call actually did. Its `events` array holds one entry per change, each `{id, type, field_name, value}` — and `value` is polymorphic across entries, a string for `status` and an integer for an id. An update that was accepted but changed nothing is visible here and nowhere else

ticket.description: The ticket **after** the update, in the same shape `zendesk-ticket-show` returns — including the new `updated_at`, which is the stamp a following safe update must send

  url = fmt("{base}/api/v2/tickets/{ticket_id}.json")
  content_type = "application/json"

parameters.description: The meeting's title, as it appears on the host's schedule and in the invitation

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Constant `2` — a scheduled, one-off meeting at a fixed time. Not caller-supplied: the recurring types need a `recurrence` object this connector cannot declare, and the instant type ignores the start time

parameters.name: start_time

nodes.name: call
nodes.title: Call
nodes.description: Invoke a registered operation with argument expressions.

nodes.name: bind
nodes.title: Bind
nodes.description: Bind the result of an expression to a symbol.

nodes.name: when
nodes.title: When
nodes.description: Conditional control flow.

nodes.name: repeat
nodes.title: Repeat
nodes.description: A bounded loop (`max` is required; the analyzer rejects unbounded loops).

nodes.name: each
nodes.title: Each
nodes.description: Map a list value through a body (list-driven loop; `repeat` stays counter-driven). Each element is bound to `as`; an optional `collect` symbol gathers the per-iteration results into a list.

nodes.name: assert
nodes.title: Assert
nodes.description: A boolean guard: aborts the flow with an error if the condition is falsey.

nodes.name: pipe
nodes.title: Pipe
nodes.description: A chain of calls where each step's output is fed as the first argument of the next.

nodes.name: seq
nodes.title: Seq
nodes.description: A sequential block; runs its body in order. Optionally binds the block's final result.

nodes.name: memo
nodes.title: Memo
nodes.description: Like `bind`, but pinned across turns: if the symbol is already resolved for this session, skip execution and reuse the cached value (compute-once-per-session, keyed on symbol name).

nodes.name: parallel
nodes.title: Parallel
nodes.description: Concurrent fan-out: run independent branches, binding each branch's result to its name.

nodes.name: await
nodes.title: Await
nodes.description: Pause until an external event/input arrives.

nodes.name: retry
nodes.title: Retry
nodes.description: Retry a body on failure with optional backoff. Fatal errors (policy denial, unknown op) are never retried. `backoff` may be `"none"` | `"linear"` | `"exponential"`.

nodes.name: try
nodes.title: Try
nodes.description: Structured error handling: run `body`; on failure bind the error string to `catch` and run `handler`. If the handler also errors, propagate that error.

nodes.name: confirm
nodes.title: Confirm
nodes.description: Explicit human-in-the-loop gate. Calls the existing `Approver` — `--yes` and TUI modal handle it automatically. Body only runs on approval; on denial the node errors. `risk` may be `"low"` | `"medium"` | `"high"` | `"critical"`.

nodes.name: loop
nodes.title: Loop
nodes.description: Time-bounded iteration. `for_ms` is required (the analyzer rejects unbounded loops). `every_ms` is the inter-iteration sleep (0 = tight). `until` is an early-exit condition.

nodes.name: race
nodes.title: Race
nodes.description: First-wins concurrency: run branches in parallel and return as soon as the first succeeds. `timeout_ms` is required; if no branch succeeds within it the node errors. `bind` names the symbol that receives the winning branch's result.

nodes.name: throttle
nodes.title: Throttle
nodes.description: Rate-limit body execution: at most `max` dispatches per `window_ms` sliding window. The token bucket is tracked in the session store keyed by `name`; plan authors declare intent, runtime enforces. `name` must be unique within a session to avoid bucket collisions.

nodes.name: debounce
nodes.title: Debounce
nodes.description: Coalesce rapid re-invocations: wait `wait_ms` after the last trigger before running body. In a `loop`/`watch` context the body only executes when things have settled. `name` is used as a stable key so debounce state survives across turns.

nodes.name: unless
nodes.title: Unless
nodes.description: Negated conditional: run `body` only when `cond` is falsey. Sugar for `when !cond`; the body may contain any nodes (reads, writes, sub-plans — anything).

nodes.name: verify
nodes.title: Verify
nodes.description: Run a command and assert its output contains an expected substring; abort the flow with a structured error if it does not. `cmd` is any node that produces a string (typically a `bash` call); `expect` is the substring the output must contain.

nodes.name: return
nodes.title: Return
nodes.description: End the flow with a value.

nodes.name: peek
nodes.title: Peek
nodes.description: Read the current in-session value of a named symbol without any filesystem IO. Returns the symbol's stored value, or an empty string if the symbol is not yet bound.

nodes.name: var
nodes.title: Var
nodes.description: Reference a bound symbol.

nodes.name: lit
nodes.title: Lit
nodes.description: A literal value (raw JSON, as written in the AST by the compiler front-end).

nodes.name: thing
nodes.title: Thing
nodes.description: A reference to an external thing.

nodes.name: expr
nodes.title: Expr
nodes.description: Pure inline computation. `formula` is a safe whitelist expression over named variables: arithmetic (`+ - * /`, `round(x,n)`, `abs`, `min`, `max`, `sum`), comparison (`== != < <= > >=`), boolean (`&& || !`, `true`/`false`, `any`, `all`, `has`), string functions (`len/lower/upper/trim/replace/repeat/reverse/contains/concat/join/split`), list helpers (`first`/`last`), string literals (`'…'`/`"…"`), lists, and objects. Dotted names such as `it.author.name` descend object fields leniently (missing/null/non-object hops read as `""`). `+` adds when both sides are numeric and concatenates otherwise. Because it yields a bool, an `expr` is also a valid `when`/`unless`/`until`/`assert` condition. `vars` maps variable names to node expressions (only `Lit` and `Var` are valid). No IO, no approval gate. Examples: `expr("price * 2", {"price": $btc})`, `expr("it.state == 'ok' && len(tags) > 0", …)`.

nodes.name: fmt
nodes.title: Fmt
nodes.description: Pure string interpolation. `template` is a string with `{name}` placeholders substituted from already-bound session symbols (same `{name}`/`{{name}}` syntax as `Lit` interpolation). No IO, no approval gate. Example: `fmt("BTC: {price} | Double: {doubled}")`.

nodes.name: jq
nodes.title: Jq
nodes.description: Pure JSON path extraction. `path` is a dot-path string (e.g. `".bitcoin.usd"` or `"results[0].value"`) applied to the JSON content of `input` (a `Var` or `Lit` node). No IO, no approval gate. Example: `jq(".bitcoin.usd", $raw)`.  `optional` selects the traversal-through-missing-data policy. When `false` — the default for native `$x.field` sugar — an absent object key, an out-of-range index, or a field access on a non-object is a loud error, so a typo'd field name fails fast instead of silently reading empty. When `true` — native `$x.field?` sugar, or a legacy JSON AST that omitted the flag — such a miss yields `null`. A present-but-`null` field is never an error in either mode.

nodes.name: parse
nodes.title: Parse
nodes.description: Pure type coercion. Converts the string result of a `jq` or `fmt` node into a typed value. `as_type` is one of `"f64"`, `"i64"`, `"bool"`, `"json"`, `"string"`. No IO, no approval gate. Example: `parse(jq(".price", $raw), as: "f64")`.

nodes.name: ctx
nodes.title: Ctx
nodes.description: Build a bounded, budgeted **context pack** from existing symbols. Resolves `include` (minus `exclude`) to its members, then — when `budget` is set — shrinks the pack *at evaluation* by visibility tier then declared order until within the char budget, recording any dropped members in the run trace. Produces a `Ctx` value bound to `name`. Pure: it selects and labels existing values, performing no IO (the load-bearing elevation of PRD §13 explicit context management).

nodes.name: ctx_append
nodes.title: Ctx Append
nodes.description: Accrete more symbols into an existing context pack (the `+=` marker). Immutably rebinds `ctx` to a *new* `Ctx` value (preserving the audit chain `$pack@1 → @2`) with `add` appended, then re-applies the pack's budget. Pure.

nodes.name: match
nodes.title: Match
nodes.description: Multi-way **exhaustive** branch: evaluate `subject` (a literal or bound symbol), then run the body of the first `case` whose `value` equals it — by JSON equality, so a *string* subject does not equal a *numeric* literal. If none match, run `default`. A deterministic replacement for chains of `when`. To branch on an op's result, bind it first (`$s = call(); match $s {…}`) or use `route`. The analyzer requires at least one case; at runtime an unmatched subject with no `default` is an error — the exhaustiveness guard-rail.

nodes.name: route
nodes.title: Route
nodes.description: Model-routed branch — the signature *bounded non-determinism* primitive. Run `selector` (typically a `!model` op) to produce a label, then run the `case` whose `label` it names. The cases are fixed and analyzer-validated: the model chooses *which* declared branch runs, never *what*. Falls back to `default` when the label matches no case (an error if `default` is empty).

nodes.name: fallback
nodes.title: Fallback
nodes.description: Ordered "first that succeeds wins" selector: run each branch in `branches` in turn; the first that completes without error and yields a non-empty result wins and becomes the node's result. On a branch error (or empty result) the next is tried — so a *side-effecting* branch that returns empty will still fall through and the next branch also runs (attempts stream live, as in `try`/`retry`). If every branch errors, the last error propagates. Lighter than `try` for graceful degradation (cheap path → else expensive path). `bind` names the winning result.

nodes.name: timeout
nodes.title: Timeout
nodes.description: Bound the wall-clock of a sub-flow: run `body` with a `ms` deadline. If it does not finish in time the node errors (an enclosing `try`/`retry` may catch it). A general reliability guard-rail you can wrap around anything. `bind` names the body's result.

nodes.name: budget
nodes.title: Budget
nodes.description: Cap the cost of a scope: run `body` but allow at most `limit` op dispatches within it (checked at statement boundaries; a nested statement can consume more than one dispatch before the next check). A first-class cost guard-rail; v1 counts dispatches (token/money budgets are a later refinement). `bind` names the body's result.

nodes.name: cap_scope
nodes.title: Cap Scope
nodes.description: **Capability scope**: run `body`, but restrict op dispatch to the tool names in `tools` — a call to anything outside that allowlist fails closed at the runtime's dispatch gate, even when the outer session policy would allow it. Capabilities only ever narrow on descent: a nested `with_tools` is intersected with the scope it's nested in, so an inner block can never re-grant a tool an outer one removed. This is the runtime-enforced counterpart of an advisory tool restriction — the analyzer also flags a literal-op `call` here that provably names a tool absent from `tools` (a static echo of the same rule dispatch enforces dynamically). `bind` names the body's result. Native text: `with_tools ["read", "grep"]` + an indented body.

nodes.name: scope
nodes.title: Scope
nodes.description: RAII-style **acquire → use → release** with guaranteed cleanup. Optionally run `acquire` first (binding its result to `bind`, so `body` and `finally` can name the resource), then run `body`; `finally` **always** runs afterward — on normal completion, an early `return`, or an error — so a lock is freed / a handle closed / a temp removed no matter how the body exits. The body's result, `return`, or error then propagates; a `finally` failure surfaces only when the body itself succeeded (it never masks the body's own error). If `acquire` errors the resource was never taken, so `finally` does not run. The deterministic resource-lifecycle guard-rail (RAII for flows).

nodes.name: saga
nodes.title: Saga
nodes.description: Saga / **compensating transaction**: run each `step` in order; after a step's `body` succeeds, its `undo` is registered. If a *later* step fails, the runtime unwinds by running the registered `undo` bodies in **reverse** order (best-effort — an `undo` failure is recorded but does not stop the unwind), then propagates the original error. The strongest guard-rail for non-transactional external side effects (charge→refund, create→delete, reserve→release): partial work is rolled back rather than left dangling. A `return` inside a step is a successful early exit and does not compensate (use `scope` for guaranteed cleanup on every exit).

nodes.name: once
nodes.title: Once
nodes.description: **At-most-once side effect** across re-runs — an effect-level `memo`. `label` is an explicit idempotency key: the first time the body runs to success in a session its result is recorded durably; later re-runs in the same session skip the body and reuse the stored result. A failed body records nothing and is retried. `bind` optionally names the body's result. Safety under re-execution (`send_email`/`charge` never fire twice). With no durable store wired (a throwaway interpreter) it degrades to running every time. Requires a non-empty literal label.

nodes.name: checkpoint
nodes.title: Checkpoint
nodes.description: **Durable resume point** for long-running / resumable flows. A **top-level-only** marker (like `await`): the first time a run reaches it, the position is recorded durably; a later re-run of the *same* flow in the *same* session fast-forwards past the already-completed prefix (its symbols are still durably bound and its side effects are not repeated) and continues from here. `label` is a human-readable name for the phase it closes. Pairs with `once` for finer-grained idempotency; a no-op when no durable store is wired. Requires a non-empty literal label.

nodes.name: obj
nodes.title: Obj
nodes.description: Build an **object value** from sub-expressions — the record constructor `{ k: expr, … }`. Each field value is itself a node, so a record can mix literals and variables: `{ ok: true, n: $count, intent: $extract.intent }`. Pure: it assembles a value, performing no IO and no op dispatch. Leaves must be pure value nodes (`var`/`lit`/`jq`/`expr`/`fmt`/`obj`/ `list`); a call or control-flow leaf is rejected by the analyzer so templates stay side-effect free. This is what lets `return { … }` assemble a result from computed symbols.

nodes.name: list
nodes.title: List
nodes.description: Build a **list value** from sub-expressions — the list constructor `[ expr, … ]`. Each item is itself a node (`[ $a, $b, 3 ]`). Pure, same leaf rules as [`Node::Obj`]; the array twin of the record constructor.

Effect.description: A side effect a tool may have.

group.description:

the model. A named group is only surfaced into the model-facing catalog when the workspace
shows evidence the group is relevant (see `flux-runtime`'s group resolver).

Branch.description:
One branch of a [`Node::Parallel`] fan-out: a named sub-flow whose final result is bound to
`name` after the branch completes. Branches should bind distinct names (the analyzer rejects
duplicates).

FallbackBranch.description: One branch of a [`Node::Fallback`]: a body tried in declared order until one succeeds.

FlowEffect.description:
A first-class *semantic* effect, declared on operations. Distinct from the host-resource
[`Effect`] (Read/Write/Network/…): a `FlowEffect` expresses execution *meaning* (this op sends
mail, costs money, irreversibly deletes) and lowers onto the host effect + a policy action via
[`FlowEffect::lower`]. Policy decides allow / deny / require-approval.

**Vocabulary invariant (C-184):** a variant names a *consequence class* — what could go wrong,
who sees it, whether it can be undone — never an application domain. "Books a meeting",
"updates a CRM record", "changes DNS" are all `send_external`/`write_db`-class consequences of
specific domains; giving each domain its own variant would grow an unbounded catalog on a
frozen wire enum. (`Calendar` predates this rule and is deprecated for exactly this reason.)

Lives here rather than in `flux-lang` because it is part of the **plugin wire vocabulary**
(`PluginManifest`'s `semantic_effects`), and a guest plugin must be able to name it without
compiling the language front-end (C-141). `flux_lang::ast` re-exports it, so the
`flux_lang::ast::FlowEffect` path used across the codebase keeps working.

oneOf.description: No effect — deterministic, side-effect free.
Reads external state.
Invokes a model (non-deterministic unless cached).
General network egress.
Writes to the filesystem.
Writes to a database / persistent store.
Sends something externally (email, message, webhook).
Irreversibly deletes.
Moves money.

Mutates a calendar.

The one application-domain noun in a consequence-class vocabulary (see the enum docs), with
zero declaration sites since day one — kept only because removing a wire enum variant fails
deserialization of any manifest that declares it, a protocol-major event.
Produces output a human will see.

MatchCase.description: One arm of a [`Node::Match`]: run `body` when the subject equals `value` (by JSON equality).

Node.description:
A node in an authored or host-derived Draft AST. Expressions and statements share one enum; the
analyzer enforces where each may appear. Agent models call native operation schemas and do not
generate this executable representation.

oneOf.description: Invoke a registered operation with argument expressions.

args.description:
Call argument expressions. For an operation with multiple declared parameters, this
array contains exactly one named object: prefer an `obj` node shaped like
`{"kind":"obj","fields":{"parameter": <value node>}}`; an object-valued `lit` is
also accepted. Never put multiple positional value nodes in this array. An operation
with exactly one required parameter may use one bare value node as shorthand.

oneOf.description: Bind the result of an expression to a symbol.
Conditional control flow.
A bounded loop (`max` is required; the analyzer rejects unbounded loops).

collect.description:
Optional symbol bound to a [`Value::List`] of each iteration's last result.
Mirrors `each`'s `collect` field for counter-driven loops.

oneOf.description:
Map a list value through a body (list-driven loop; `repeat` stays counter-driven). Each element
is bound to `as`; an optional `collect` symbol gathers the per-iteration results into a list.

as.description: The symbol bound to each element inside the body.

collect.description:
Optional symbol bound to a [`Value::List`] of each iteration's result.
When `flat` is `true` the collected values are flattened one level
(each iteration must produce a list; the results are concatenated).

flat.description:
If `true` and `collect` is set, flatten the per-iteration results
(each must be a list) into one combined list instead of a list-of-lists.

in.description: The list to iterate (an expression yielding a [`Value::List`]).

oneOf.description: A boolean guard: aborts the flow with an error if the condition is falsey.
A chain of calls where each step's output is fed as the first argument of the next.

bind.description: Optional symbol bound to the chain's final result.

oneOf.description: A sequential block; runs its body in order. Optionally binds the block's final result.

Like `bind`, but pinned across turns: if the symbol is already resolved for this session, skip
execution and reuse the cached value (compute-once-per-session, keyed on symbol name).
Concurrent fan-out: run independent branches, binding each branch's result to its name.
Pause until an external event/input arrives.

condition.description:
Optional pure condition. A false condition skips this top-level suspension point; this
keeps decision points authored and durable without nesting `await` inside control flow.

oneOf.description:
Retry a body on failure with optional backoff. Fatal errors (policy denial, unknown op) are
never retried. `backoff` may be `"none"` | `"linear"` | `"exponential"`.

Structured error handling: run `body`; on failure bind the error string to `catch` and run
`handler`. If the handler also errors, propagate that error.

Explicit human-in-the-loop gate. Calls the existing `Approver` — `--yes` and TUI modal
handle it automatically. Body only runs on approval; on denial the node errors.
`risk` may be `"low"` | `"medium"` | `"high"` | `"critical"`.

Time-bounded iteration. `for_ms` is required (the analyzer rejects unbounded loops).
`every_ms` is the inter-iteration sleep (0 = tight). `until` is an early-exit condition.

First-wins concurrency: run branches in parallel and return as soon as the first
succeeds. `timeout_ms` is required; if no branch succeeds within it the node errors.
`bind` names the symbol that receives the winning branch's result.

Rate-limit body execution: at most `max` dispatches per `window_ms` sliding window.
The token bucket is tracked in the session store keyed by `name`; plan authors declare intent,
runtime enforces. `name` must be unique within a session to avoid bucket collisions.

name.description: Stable bucket name — keyed in the session store so the limit persists across turns.

oneOf.description:
Coalesce rapid re-invocations: wait `wait_ms` after the last trigger before running body.
In a `loop`/`watch` context the body only executes when things have settled.
`name` is used as a stable key so debounce state survives across turns.

name.description: Stable key name for this debounce site.

oneOf.description:
Negated conditional: run `body` only when `cond` is falsey. Sugar for `when !cond`;
the body may contain any nodes (reads, writes, sub-plans — anything).

Run a command and assert its output contains an expected substring; abort the flow with a
structured error if it does not. `cmd` is any node that produces a string (typically a
`bash` call); `expect` is the substring the output must contain.
End the flow with a value.

Read the current in-session value of a named symbol without any filesystem IO.
Returns the symbol's stored value, or an empty string if the symbol is not yet bound.
Reference a bound symbol.
A literal value (raw JSON, as written in the AST by the compiler front-end).
A reference to an external thing.

Pure inline computation. `formula` is a safe whitelist expression over named variables:
arithmetic (`+ - * /`, `round(x,n)`, `abs`, `min`, `max`, `sum`), comparison
(`== != < <= > >=`), boolean (`&& || !`, `true`/`false`, `any`, `all`, `has`), string
functions (`len/lower/upper/trim/replace/repeat/reverse/contains/concat/join/split`), list
helpers (`first`/`last`), string literals (`'…'`/`"…"`), lists, and objects. Dotted names
such as `it.author.name` descend object fields leniently (missing/null/non-object hops read
as `""`). `+` adds when both sides are numeric and concatenates otherwise. Because it yields a
bool, an `expr` is also a valid `when`/`unless`/`until`/`assert` condition. `vars` maps
variable names to node expressions (only `Lit` and `Var` are valid). No IO, no approval gate.
Examples: `expr("price * 2", {"price": $btc})`, `expr("it.state == 'ok' && len(tags) > 0", …)`.

Pure string interpolation. `template` is a string with `{name}` placeholders substituted
from already-bound session symbols (same `{name}`/`{{name}}` syntax as `Lit` interpolation).
No IO, no approval gate. Example: `fmt("BTC: {price} | Double: {doubled}")`.

Pure JSON path extraction. `path` is a dot-path string (e.g. `".bitcoin.usd"` or
`"results[0].value"`) applied to the JSON content of `input` (a `Var` or `Lit` node).
No IO, no approval gate. Example: `jq(".bitcoin.usd", $raw)`.

`optional` selects the traversal-through-missing-data policy. When `false` — the
default for native `$x.field` sugar — an absent object key, an out-of-range index, or a field
access on a non-object is a loud error, so a typo'd field name fails fast instead of silently
reading empty. When `true` — native `$x.field?` sugar, or a legacy JSON AST that omitted the
flag — such a miss yields `null`. A present-but-`null` field is never an error in either mode.

Pure type coercion. Converts the string result of a `jq` or `fmt` node into a typed
value. `as_type` is one of `"f64"`, `"i64"`, `"bool"`, `"json"`, `"string"`.
No IO, no approval gate. Example: `parse(jq(".price", $raw), as: "f64")`.

Build a bounded, budgeted **context pack** from existing symbols. Resolves `include` (minus
`exclude`) to its members, then — when `budget` is set — shrinks the pack *at evaluation* by
visibility tier then declared order until within the char budget, recording any dropped members
in the run trace. Produces a `Ctx` value bound to `name`. Pure: it selects and labels existing
values, performing no IO (the load-bearing elevation of PRD §13 explicit context management).

Accrete more symbols into an existing context pack (the `+=` marker). Immutably rebinds `ctx`
to a *new* `Ctx` value (preserving the audit chain `$pack@1 → @2`) with `add` appended, then
re-applies the pack's budget. Pure.

Multi-way **exhaustive** branch: evaluate `subject` (a literal or bound symbol), then run the
body of the first `case` whose `value` equals it — by JSON equality, so a *string* subject does
not equal a *numeric* literal. If none match, run `default`. A deterministic replacement for
chains of `when`. To branch on an op's result, bind it first (`$s = call(); match $s {…}`) or
use `route`. The analyzer requires at least one case; at runtime an unmatched subject with no
`default` is an error — the exhaustiveness guard-rail.

Model-routed branch — the signature *bounded non-determinism* primitive. Run `selector`
(typically a `!model` op) to produce a label, then run the `case` whose `label` it names. The
cases are fixed and analyzer-validated: the model chooses *which* declared branch runs, never
*what*. Falls back to `default` when the label matches no case (an error if `default` is empty).

Ordered "first that succeeds wins" selector: run each branch in `branches` in turn; the first
that completes without error and yields a non-empty result wins and becomes the node's result.
On a branch error (or empty result) the next is tried — so a *side-effecting* branch that
returns empty will still fall through and the next branch also runs (attempts stream live, as
in `try`/`retry`). If every branch errors, the last error propagates. Lighter than `try` for
graceful degradation (cheap path → else expensive path). `bind` names the winning result.

Bound the wall-clock of a sub-flow: run `body` with a `ms` deadline. If it does not finish in
time the node errors (an enclosing `try`/`retry` may catch it). A general reliability
guard-rail you can wrap around anything. `bind` names the body's result.

Cap the cost of a scope: run `body` but allow at most `limit` op dispatches within it (checked
at statement boundaries; a nested statement can consume more than one dispatch before the next
check). A first-class cost guard-rail; v1 counts dispatches (token/money budgets are a later
refinement). `bind` names the body's result.

**Capability scope**: run `body`, but restrict op dispatch to the tool names in `tools` — a
call to anything outside that allowlist fails closed at the runtime's dispatch gate, even when
the outer session policy would allow it. Capabilities only ever narrow on descent: a nested
`with_tools` is intersected with the scope it's nested in, so an inner block can never re-grant
a tool an outer one removed. This is the runtime-enforced counterpart of an advisory tool
restriction — the analyzer also flags a literal-op `call` here that provably names a tool absent
from `tools` (a static echo of the same rule dispatch enforces dynamically). `bind` names the
body's result. Native text: `with_tools ["read", "grep"]` + an indented body.

RAII-style **acquire → use → release** with guaranteed cleanup. Optionally run `acquire`
first (binding its result to `bind`, so `body` and `finally` can name the resource), then run
`body`; `finally` **always** runs afterward — on normal completion, an early `return`, or an
error — so a lock is freed / a handle closed / a temp removed no matter how the body exits.
The body's result, `return`, or error then propagates; a `finally` failure surfaces only when
the body itself succeeded (it never masks the body's own error). If `acquire` errors the
resource was never taken, so `finally` does not run. The deterministic resource-lifecycle
guard-rail (RAII for flows).

Saga / **compensating transaction**: run each `step` in order; after a step's `body` succeeds,
its `undo` is registered. If a *later* step fails, the runtime unwinds by running the registered
`undo` bodies in **reverse** order (best-effort — an `undo` failure is recorded but does not stop
the unwind), then propagates the original error. The strongest guard-rail for non-transactional
external side effects (charge→refund, create→delete, reserve→release): partial work is rolled
back rather than left dangling. A `return` inside a step is a successful early exit and does not
compensate (use `scope` for guaranteed cleanup on every exit).

**At-most-once side effect** across re-runs — an effect-level `memo`. `label` is an explicit
idempotency key: the first time the body runs to success in a session its result is recorded
durably; later re-runs in the same session skip the body and reuse the stored result. A failed
body records nothing and is retried. `bind` optionally names the body's result. Safety under
re-execution (`send_email`/`charge` never fire twice). With no durable store wired (a throwaway
interpreter) it degrades to running every time. Requires a non-empty literal label.

**Durable resume point** for long-running / resumable flows. A **top-level-only** marker (like
`await`): the first time a run reaches it, the position is recorded durably; a later re-run of
the *same* flow in the *same* session fast-forwards past the already-completed prefix (its
symbols are still durably bound and its side effects are not repeated) and continues from here.
`label` is a human-readable name for the phase it closes. Pairs with `once` for finer-grained
idempotency; a no-op when no durable store is wired. Requires a non-empty literal label.

Build an **object value** from sub-expressions — the record constructor `{ k: expr, … }`. Each
field value is itself a node, so a record can mix literals and variables:
`{ ok: true, n: $count, intent: $extract.intent }`. Pure: it assembles a value, performing no
IO and no op dispatch. Leaves must be pure value nodes (`var`/`lit`/`jq`/`expr`/`fmt`/`obj`/
`list`); a call or control-flow leaf is rejected by the analyzer so templates stay side-effect
free. This is what lets `return { … }` assemble a result from computed symbols.

Build a **list value** from sub-expressions — the list constructor `[ expr, … ]`. Each item is
itself a node (`[ $a, $b, 3 ]`). Pure, same leaf rules as [`Node::Obj`]; the array twin of the
record constructor.

RouteCase.description: One arm of a [`Node::Route`]: run `body` when the selector yields the string `label`.

SagaStep.description:
One step of a [`Node::Saga`]: a `body` of forward work plus the `undo` that compensates it if a
*later* step fails. `undo` may be empty — an irreversible or read-only step registers no
compensation and is simply skipped during an unwind.

Selector.description: How a thing is addressed before resolution.

SymbolName.description: A session symbol name (the `$draft` in source is stored without the `$`).

ThingKind.description: The kind of an addressable external object.

oneOf.description: A domain-specific kind.

ThingRef.description: An unresolved reference to an external object.

TypeRef.description:
A (deliberately small) type reference. The analyzer checks op signatures against these; richer
structural typing can grow here later.

oneOf.description: The top type — matches anything (used before inference).
A homogeneous list.
A named/registered type (struct schema, op output type, …).

flux_ast.description:
The Draft AST: an optionally-named, parameterized flow with a body. May contain unresolved
symbols and thing references until the analyzer runs.
